item.title: Trump says Zelensky 'doesn't want to end this war' after Ukraine hits Russian terminal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US President Donald Trump has excoriated Ukraine ’s leader after the country launched one of its biggest drone attacks on Russia this year, hitting a key oil terminal in defiance of his demand it stop hitting Russian energy infrastructure. There have been growing tensions between Ukraine and the US in recent days, prompting fears in Kyiv it could lose essential support as it approaches another winter under relentless Russian attack. Trump on Friday invoked a waiver exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky later told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the US siding with Russia would be a “historic mistake.” Smoke rises above the city following an air attack on the oil terminal in Saint Petersburg, Russia, on Sunday. - AFP/Getty Images In the wake of Ukraine’s drone attack overnight into Sunday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that he doesn’t want to do anything that will drive Russia away from negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, adding that he believes “great progress is being made.” At the same time, he hit out at Zelensky, saying that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did” – a claim firmly rejected by Zelensky. “I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote in the post Sunday. Despite this, the Ukrainian president said he spoke to US envoy, Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Sunday as part of “nonstop communication” aimed at securing long-term peace. “We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer,” Zelensky posted on X . Meanwhile, news of a potential trilateral meeting between Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on ending Russia’s war with Ukraine risks escalating tensions further. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Monday that any future meeting between the three leaders would “encourage Putin to continue this war,” after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio touted possible talks. Rubio, who is currently on a visit to Uzbekistan, had been asked by a reporter there about a Wall Street Journal report that Putin had floated such a summit in a phone call with Trump earlier this month. He responded: “Well, I don’t know. I mean, I think there’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know if anything’s been finalized.” The Kremlin said Monday that “given that all three heads of state might potentially take part in the summit in China, the topic of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed mentioned.” “However, no concrete proposals or agreements – neither regarding the meeting itself nor its potential agenda and content – have been discussed or put forward by anyone,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters. A spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said, “I have no information to share at the moment.” Ukraine targets oil sites Ukraine is keeping up long-range strikes into Russia. Russia’s defense ministry said it shot down 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight into Sunday over various parts of the country. One target was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, according to Russian authorities. The terminal can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year. Ukraine’s Fire Point company, which makes the drones used in the attack, said there was a fire on the terminal’s grounds following the strike. A logistics centers in St. Petersburg was also attacked, according to Ozon, a Russian distribution company, as well as a data center for the Russian VKontakte social media platform. One person was killed and five wounded in the attacks, with residential homes damaged as well, according to local authorities. “They shot one down right above us: there was one bright flash, and it shook us up quite strongly,” a 41-year old resident of St. Petersburg told CNN. “I heard a roar, got everyone out of their beds, took the cat, and we hid in the bathroom,” another said. A deepening spat Ukraine’s strikes come amid Zelensky’s deteriorating relationship with Trump, who last week called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace.” A week ago, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure, as the White House tries to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices ahead of crucial midterm elections. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such an agreement. Ukraine briefly halted such attacks, but Russia never stopped pounding Ukraine’s energy plants and cities. Eleven people were killed and nearly 50 injured across Ukraine in Russian missile and drone attacks in the 24 hours to Sunday morning, according to Ukrainian authorities, including what they called a massive attack on energy facilities in the Odesa region. “Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ​ago, Russia has ​deliberately ‌attacked ​Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors ⁠76 times,” Zelensky ​wrote on X Sunday. People watch the burning oil terminal following an air attack in Saint Petersburg, Russia, on October 18, 2026. - AFP/Getty Images Trump has waived sanctions on imports of Russian diesel and on Friday invoked a waiver exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress, sparking criticism even from Republicans . In an interview Sunday with “Meet the Press,” Zelensky said the waiver strengthened Putin’s war against Ukraine while Moscow was failing on the battlefield. He also repeated that the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink system to guide its short-range and battlefield drones was still curtailed. “It was a message from the American government” to limit the speed at which Ukrainian drones could fly, Zelensky said. The Trump administration has denied it ordered the service restricted. No early warnings Zelensky said that intelligence sharing had been blocked by the US side for three days during ballistic missile attacks but had since been restored. In response, Rubio said: “I don’t know where (Zelensky’s) getting these things from or why he’s saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There’s been no pause.” US satellite networks have been critical in providing the Ukrainian military with warnings of incoming missiles. According to Zelensky, Ukraine received no early warning before a ballistic missile attack multiple times within the last week. “Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” he posted on X Monday. He also reaffirmed Kyiv’s commitment to a long-term peace deal. “Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end,” he said. In his Sunday interview, Zelensky was also asked about Trump’s comments that he was more difficult to deal with than Putin and replied it was “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.” Zelensky said he wanted to trust Trump and hoped he would change his attitude to Putin. Asked if Trump was an ally of Ukraine, Zelensky said: “I hope so.” CNN’s Daria Tarasova, Julia Benbrook, Logan Schiciano, Billy Stockwell, Anna Chernova and Jennifer Hanlser contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/18/europe/ukraine-russia-drone-attack-trump-intl

item.title: Democrats may have an unlikely ally in a post-midterms effort to oust Hegseth
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Senate Democrats are quietly floating the ouster of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth after the Nov. 3 election as the political price for cooperation on key defense-related issues in the postelection lame-duck session, and they may have some GOP support to shake up the Pentagon’s leadership, according to Senate sources. The Defense Department has set recruiting records under Hegseth’s leadership, and the Pentagon chief appears to have strong support from President Trump, who likes to brag that Hegseth looks like a military leader from “central casting.” But some Republican senators haven’t been happy with Hegseth’s leadership, especially his ouster of well-respected military leaders such as Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, Army chief of staff Randy George, Navy Secretary John Phelan and four-star Gen. Chris Donahue, the top U.S. military officer in Europe. Democrats view Hegseth’s leadership as a disaster and are looking for leverage to push him out after the midterm elections, according to Senate sources, just as they attempted to push former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem out of her job during the prolonged stalemate over funding for her department earlier this year. Trump eventually fired Noem after key Republican senators, such as Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), turned against her publicly. Now Democrats have significant leverage over Hegseth’s future at the Pentagon as they’re threatening to hold up emergency defense funding the White House requested in June as well as regular funding for the Defense Department, which expires on Dec. 11. Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hegseth’s resignation could set the stage for more bipartisan cooperation on must-pass defense bills, such as the National Defense Authorization Act and the annual defense appropriations bill. Kaine told The Hill before the Senate adjourned for the election that Hegseth’s departure would help lower the partisan temperature in the standoff over the defense measures. Republican sources say that Senate Democrats have already privately floated Hegseth’s termination as something that could help muster bipartisan cooperation on filling key vacancies at the Pentagon, such as the positions of Army and Navy secretary left open by the departures of Driscoll and Phelan. As things now stand, Senate Democrats are threatening to block the defense spending bills and also a waiver for Hung Cao, Trump’s nominee to serve as Navy secretary. Cao needs a special congressional waiver to lead the Navy because federal law requires a seven-year waiting period before former military officers can be confirmed to top Pentagon civilian leadership posts. Democrats are drawing a hard line on supporting defense funding in the lame-duck session if the military conflict with Iran isn’t wrapped up before the end of the year. “My own view is that if the war is over, then the opportunity for bipartisanship on defense authorization and defense appropriations is there. I think if the war’s not over, it’s going to be extremely difficult,” said Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is poised to take over as Democratic whip in the next Congress. Schatz said he was speaking about his personal view of the prospects of a deal on defense spending. So far, some key Senate Republicans say they don’t see Trump agreeing to push Hegseth out of the job to get cooperation from Democrats on the defense authorization and funding measures in the lame-duck session. “That’s a bridge too far,” warned a GOP senator, who requested anonymity to discuss the looming negotiations over breaking the logjam on defense legislation after Election Day. A senior Pentagon official dismissed the criticism of Hegseth’s leadership from Democrats and some key Republicans by pointing to his record of accomplishments over the past 20 months. “Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength,” the official said in response to jockeying by Democrats to push Hegseth out of his role, using the Trump administration's preferred name for the Department of Defense. “Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all-time highs. Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way. By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before,” the senior official said. “The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.” There are growing questions, however, on Capitol Hill about whether Trump and Hegseth are fully in sync on several important issues. Trump recently cancelled Hegseth’s plan to run a livestream of the execution of Maj. Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 at a mass shooting at Fort Hood in 2009. There’s also confusion about whether Hegseth or other senior Pentagon officials directed a temporary halt to intelligence sharing with Ukraine or ordered the restriction of Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite-based internet network, without Trump’s knowledge and approval. Four Republican senators — Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (Maine), Sen. John Cornyn (Texas), Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.) and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) — signed a bipartisan letter last week directing the Defense Department inspector general, Platte Moring, demanding he immediately investigate whether any Pentagon officials “directed” or “authorized” changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine. Collins has separately faulted Hegseth for not fully anticipating that Iran would be able to shut down most shipping traffic, including nearly a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil supply, through the vulnerable Strait of Hormuz in response to U.S. and Israeli attacks. “For example, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz should have been anticipated. It happened during the Iraq-Iran war and it’s an obvious point of leverage but there doesn’t seem to have been any plan for it,” Collins said last month. Tillis wrote in his new memoir that his decision to cast a deciding vote to confirm Hegseth in January 2025 is “the biggest regret of my career.” Some Republicans already acknowledge that pushing Hegseth out of his job in the lame-duck session could avoid a messy impeachment battle next year, aside from paving the way for a potential deal on the defense authorization and appropriations bills before Christmas. “Trump should fire Hegseth to avoid Hegseth’s impeachment. It’s the honorable thing to do,” Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) posted Thursday on the social platform X. The maverick conservative who lost his primary reelection bid earlier this year when Trump endorsed his opponent noted that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) had to scramble to avoid voting on Hegseth’s impeachment before the election. “The House recessed early to avoid the vote, so I will reintroduce Hegseth articles of impeachment when we return for the lame duck session, regardless of the outcome of the midterm election,” House Democrats, led by Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April. Democrats in the lower chamber plan to make Hegseth a top political target next year if they win the majority in next month’s election, something that political handicappers project is likely. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) told Semafor that impeaching Hegseth should be one of House Democrats’ “top three priorities” next year. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. item.title: Obama condemns comments by 'border czar' that Ilhan Omar could be denaturalized
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Homeland security officers carry boxes from the Washington DC residence of Ilhan Omar, on 12 October. Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/AP Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her. Obama wrote Sunday morning, on X , that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.” He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs, adding: “if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her – or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.” Obama, too, has had his citizenship scrutinized by Trump, who more than a decade ago fueled false conspiracy theories that Obama was born in Kenya and therefore not eligible to be president. Related: Ilhan Omar’s attorneys say federal search of her home was ‘neither justified nor lawful’ Tom Homan , Trump’s “border czar”, was asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”. “If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before. “And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.” Homan’s comments were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a top Trump administration official since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October. The search of Omar’s home sparked major backlash and accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized about denaturalizing and deporting . The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the November midterm elections , in which Omar is on the ballot. Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details. “I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.” Omar – a naturalized US citizen from Somalia – was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020. Obama stated in his post on X that Omar arrived in the US with her father when she was 12, and five years later, when her father became a naturalized citizen, she became one, too, because she was 17. (An 18-year-old would have had to apply for citizenship separately, he noted.) “Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” he wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone – all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.” In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneys accused the US justice department of potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy. The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its offensive on legal migration . The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship. As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings. Nonetheless, as of April, the US justice department had reportedly identified nearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate. The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also include allegations that her ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US. Related: Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says The federal government reportedly seized Omar’s phone during the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives. Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search. Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers. There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal . Even veterans at the Department of Justice expressed shock over the targeting of Omar, according to reporting by NBC News . “I was astounded to see a search of a sitting congressperson this close to an election,” said Peter Carr, a former career justice department spokesperson, NBC News reported. “Historically, the department has been very adamant that politics plays no role in investigative decisions they make and they try very hard to avoid taking overt actions that might even have the perception of influencing an election.” After the raid on her home, Omar posted on X that she was “ok”. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” “I will not be silenced,” Omar added. This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/trump-border-czar-says-ilhan-171602251.html

item.title: Republicans already know who they want to blame if they suffer big midterm losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans are already starting to blame each other as the midterm election spirals further out of their control. Everyone is bracing for President Donald Trump's ire if the party loses big in November. House Republicans are planning to accuse the Senate side. Trump political aides have taken to directly calling campaigns they feel aren't performing well enough. National GOP operatives are quietly furious at lackluster candidates who didn't do enough to prepare for a tough year despite early warnings. And some GOP candidates are pointing the finger back at their own party committees. It's a vicious cycle, according to more than a dozen top GOP operatives and lawmakers who spoke to POLITICO, some of whom were granted anonymity to candidly discuss private conversations. “If it happens, there will be plenty of blame to go around,” said Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R-N.J.), who is in his own tighter-than-comfortable race. That Republicans have already spent significant time gaming out the aftermath and how to insulate themselves from the fallout of what they fear will be significant GOP losses illustrates how precarious the current landscape is for the party. That’s even as top Republicans publicly insist they are bullish on keeping control of both chambers in Congress. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who is widely expected to be the next National Republican Senatorial Committee chair, told reporters Thursday that “if the Democrats do win the House and the Senate, it won't be because of their left-wing lunatic candidates, it'll be because people are pissed off about gas prices, and I get that.” House Republicans are annoyed with Senate Republicans for fumbling a once-safe GOP map as well as creating top-of-the-ticket drag for them with bad candidates in some key states — but senators privately put the onus on Trump for forcing out better Republican incumbents and then backing flawed GOP candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas , according to three GOP senators and a national GOP operative. The top Senate GOP Super PAC and Trump’s MAGA Inc. have spent nearly $200 million alone to save Paxton, who’s locked in a tight race with Democrat James Talarico. Trump, for his part, has already landed on who to blame in the event of a Paxton loss next month. “If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday afternoon , targeting the Texas senator he endorsed against in the primary in Cornyn, and a longtime GOP foe in Rove. There’s also particular frustration with Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who numerous GOP operatives grumbled never took his race seriously and is now costing the party millions of dollars to rescue in a state Democrats haven’t won in almost a century. Marshall’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. “No one in the world expected that the Senate would need as much money as they did,” said one national GOP operative working on multiple competitive House races. “All of this money that was expected to go to the House, for the most part, is now being wasted on the Senate because they fucked up so bad.” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle blasted “armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation” and said Trump “is laser-focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress this November, which is why he is traveling across the country highlighting the historic victories his Administration has delivered for the American people.” “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction,” Ingle said. “Those who are actually involved with Republicans' midterm strategy remain laser-focused on winning races and are confident we are still in a position to protect and expand our majorities," said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. A slew of troubling internal GOP polling in recent weeks set off a new level of panic across House GOP leadership, political operations and individual campaigns. It didn’t just reveal a harsh environment for the party in power on par with typical midterms, but potentially catastrophic scenarios in formerly safe red seats across the country. Even top House Republicans expect to lose the House majority at this point. A growing group of Hill Republicans argue the blame rests with Trump, and his decisions to get the U.S. into an open-ended war with Iran that has driven up fuel prices, while enacting a slew of tariffs and other policy moves that have riled farmers. “I’ve talked to some who are making these decisions: The biggest problem is the president’s polling numbers and unfavorables,” retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) recently told POLITICO . Still, not everyone is blaming Trump: In an explosive move this week, GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, who is close with the president and faces her own surprisingly competitive race, accused the National Republican Congressional Committee of dropping the ball. “I am also getting calls from members wondering what is going on at the @NRCC,” Luna posted on social media , adding she was also getting inquiries about House leadership races. “Sounds to me like some in leadership need to focus on winning races instead of gaming their next steak donor dinner.” Some rank-and-file Republicans are frustrated the NRCC didn’t pivot faster to trying to shore up at-risk GOP incumbents across the map as the landscape deteriorated in August and September. “The leadership at the NRCC is living in a bubble,” another House Republican said. “We’re getting killed out here.” Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, noted that the committee moved early to launch coordinated advertising campaigns with incumbents in districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.), Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.), Rob Wittman (R-Va.), Mike Turner (R-Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas). To date, the NRCC has run coordinated advertising in 51 districts, Marinella said. GOP lawmakers and operatives working to defend the party’s majorities in Congress have been discussing amongst themselves how to avoid being thrown under the bus come Nov. 3, according to a dozen of the people interviewed. The rising tensions have also turned up in the rather intense shadow leadership race underway within Speaker Mike Johnson’s circle and the senior ranks of the House GOP, with opposing camps preparing to blame each other, according to five of the people. GOP Whip Tom Emmer has said publicly that some of the GOP redistricting efforts won’t work, and Republicans won’t win all those seats. Trump officials have also been feeling the pressure, sometimes calling campaigns to try to revive lagging operations or attempting to install new staff within them, according to two Republicans familiar with the matter. In another stunning move, Trump officials are warning Republicans that pro-Trump super PACs can only help so much and the candidates need to shift their strategy to a positive message and a list of key deliverables for voters — or they will lose. “Republican success in many cases is going to hinge on the following: do they give voters a reason to vote for them?” a senior Republican official familiar with MAGA Inc.’s plans said. “They're being inundated with reasons to vote against the Democrats, and in many places they already instinctually want to. But are they given a reason to actually vote for the Republicans to show up and vote?” The person added that “the number one thing that every Republican in the country” should be doing in the final weeks is laying out “things that they are going to do to tangibly improve people's personal economic situation and their life” and “lower your cost of living.” “If Republicans are failing to lay out a reason to come vote for them and saying, ‘Here's what I, as a candidate, am for, what I am going to do to make your economics better,’ there’s a good chance they're going to lose,” the Republican official warned. That assessment has shocked several Republicans in tough races. It’s a big shift from even how House leadership has approached the campaign trail: Johnson has spent the last few weeks hammering a message of contrast between his party of “common sense” and Democrats as a party of dangerous socialists who will investigate the president and empower America’s “enemies” if they win. “We’re running for our lives,” another House Republican in a tough race said. “Those are two totally different approaches. And we have two weeks.” Erin Doherty contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/republican-knives-out-midterms-trump-01124859

item.title: AI is making politicians say things they didn't in attack ads that are already airing
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Illustration: Shoshana Gordon/Axios AI is producing reality-bending midterm ads about defaced Bibles, upscale dinners and a board game with a "Death to America" playing card. Why it matters: The warnings about deepfakes are coming true. Election laws haven't kept pace with a world where campaigns can put words in opponents' mouths and create realistic-looking scenes that didn't happen. The Wesleyan Media Project found $137 million had been spent on 220 AI-generated ads through Oct. 11, mostly from Republicans. Four states have laws prohibiting certain uses of AI-generated deepfakes in political ads, while 27 more require some form of disclosure about their use. No federal law specifically regulates AI-generated political ads. The big picture: An Axios analysis found numerous political ads partly or fully made by generative AI, sometimes undisclosed. Georgia Senate: Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans, has run a series of AI-generated deepfake ads depicting Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff getting beauty treatments. The ads mock Ossoff's reported campaign spending on hair and makeup , saying he "talks pretty" but has "an ugly record" and "a lot to cover up." Ossoff said in a C-SPAN interview : "It is deeply troubling to see ... deepfake videos used to fabricate political advertising. And it's a s lippery slope toward the destruction of truth in political debate, and the ad should come down immediately." The ads don't disclose AI use, which Georgia law doesn't require. Michigan Senate: A super PAC called Front Line Action used AI in an ad depicting Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo with podcaster Hasan Piker and four women wearing niqabs. Another AI-generated scene has El-Sayed playing a Risk-style board game with his half-sister , Eman Abdelhadi, and Piker. It depicts cards bearing statements that include "Death to America," "Do not Celebrate Thanksgiving" and "Celebrate 9/11." The group has defended the ad, telling CNN it is "grounded in El-Sayed's own public statements and documented reporting and records concerning him and individuals associated with or supportive of his campaign." The ad features both a written and spoken disclosure that it was "created in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence." New York governor: Republican Bruce Blakeman's campaign and allied super PACs have repeatedly used generative AI in ads attacking Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, with varying degrees of disclosure. One AI-generated ad released by the Blakeman campaign depicts the Tooth Fairy struggling to come up with cash to give to children, saying she "just can't afford to be the Tooth Fairy in Kathy Hochul's New York." Another Blakesman spot says onscreen: "We asked AI what a truthful Kathy Hochul ad would look like." The ad features AI-generated scenes of Hochul attending an upscale dinner and standing outside a police precinct while a man asks her: "Want some crack?" Pennsylvania governor: A new ad from Republican candidate Stacy Garrity features an AI-generated version of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro talking about taxes, abortion and data centers. The spot puts this quote in his mouth: "This ad was created with AI, thanks to big, beautiful data centers. Fact is, I was the one who fast-tracked data centers right here in PA, right after they handed me $5 million in political contributions." Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder, in a statement to Axios, dismissed the ad as "cheap, dishonest AI bullshit." Texas Senate: Democratic candidate James Talarico has been a consistent target of AI-generated ads from both Republican Ken Paxton's campaign and outside super PACs. A Paxton campaign ad uses AI to depict Talarico defacing a Bible with crayon and saying, "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were." Talarico told NBC he "tried in the legislature to ban AI deepfake videos in political campaigns because they are misleading. They are lying about a candidate in this race." Kentucky's 6th District: No Going Back PAC, backed by President Trump's MAGA Inc., has run several ads using AI to boost Republican congressional candidate Ralph Alvarado. One ad features multiple AI-generated deepfakes of Democrat Zach Dembo, including one scene in which he stares into the camera. item.title: Supreme Court agrees to review Reconstruction-era ban on distilling spirits in private homes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to consider whether Congress had the constitutional authority to impose a ban on distilling spirits in private homes more than 150 years ago. Plaintiffs challenging the prohibition on home distilling claim the 1868 law is an antiquated relic of Reconstruction-era politics. They argue that Congress overstepped its taxation powers when it enacted the home distilling ban as part of a tax reform measure designed to curb fraud by commercial distillers. Government attorneys counter that Congress properly restricted where spirits can be distilled to prevent producers from evading federal excise taxes. They warn that lifting the ban would violate Supreme Court precedent and erode congressional powers. Federal law makes home distilling a crime punishable by a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. Separate challenges to the law divided two federal circuit courts, which issued conflicting decisions in April, only 11 days apart. A three-judge panel from the Sixth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the federal ban in a case brought by John Ream, a brewpub owner from Newark, Ohio, who wants to distill whisky at home for his personal consumption. A Fifth Circuit panel ruled in favor of different plaintiffs — members of the Texas-based Hobby Distillers Association — and concluded that statutory prohibitions on in-home distilling are outside the scope of Congress’ taxing power under the Constitution. The Supreme Court agreed to review the Fifth Circuit decision, which was the Justice Department’s preference. Plaintiffs’ attorney Robert Alt said they are “thrilled” that the Supreme Court agreed to hear the case. “Our country’s founders would be rolling over in their graves to learn that a pastime in which even George Washington partook, which is as American as apple pie and certainly a lot older, has quite absurdly been turned into a federal crime,” Alt said in a statement. Attorneys for the plaintiffs in both cases argue that Congress could ban a broad array of activities inside private homes — including cooking, gardening and remote work — under the government’s interpretation of the 19th century law. “The importance of this case and the questions it presents could hardly be overstated,” the plaintiffs' lawyers wrote . “It presents fundamental questions of the extent of federal power and the powers reserved to the states and the people.” Justice Department attorneys said the government’s regulation and taxation on the production of distilled spirits is as old as Congress itself. They noted that Congress outlawed home distilling to prevent those producers from evading taxes or government inspections. “And because the location restrictions were enacted only after lengthy experience with tax evasion, upholding those restrictions would not open the door to hypothetical laws restricting other conduct lacking that history,” they wrote . The government says Ream asked the Supreme Court to resolve an “additional question” of whether location restrictions on home distilling exceed the scope of Congress’s power to regulate interstate commerce. But the government urged the high court to avoid that question, saying it wasn’t part of Ream’s case or the government’s current arguments in either case. ___ Follow the AP's coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court . item.title: Justice Dept. is suing 30 states over voter data. Even Republicans are pushing back.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
With midterm elections just two weeks away, there are concerns that the federal government's pressure on election officials is breeding distrust in the system. Federal agents have seized ballots , and voting machines have been examined. The Justice Department is locked in legal battles with states across the country over information about individual voters and this past week threatened to prosecute California election officials if they knowingly count mail-in ballots from 20,000 people the Trump administration says are "likely noncitizens." It's a kind of interference Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, a Republican in a deeply red state, said she's never seen before. "In the past two elections that I oversaw as lieutenant governor, the threats were all external: non-state actors, cyber security threats and other things," she said. "But now we also have threats coming from within our own government." Federal government actions on elections In the U.S., elections are local. They're run by towns and counties and states. It's stated in Article I of the Constitution. Congress makes laws regulating elections, but the president doesn't have a role in running them. Still, during his second term Mr. Trump has signed two executive orders around voting: one requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and another on mail-in ballots . The administration's latest move came Thursday, when the Justice Department sued California , claiming it was mailing ballots to more than 20,000 likely noncitizens. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said the federal government was threatening the right of thousands of Californians to vote without providing any detail about how they identified those individuals, and she questioned the accuracy of the data. The Justice Department's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber said in a statement . "Noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections," head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division Harmeet Dhillon told 60 Minutes. "So the question is simply how many of them there are." Demands for voter rolls Last year the Justice Department asked nearly every state in the country for their full and complete voter rolls, including confidential voter information. "They wanted things that we typically are required by law to keep private: social security numbers, full dates of birth, driver's license numbers," said Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, who is responsible for Utah's elections. Henderson told 60 Minutes she wasn't given good answers about why the federal government wanted the information, and she was concerned about what would be done with the data. She refused to turn them over. Officials in 29 other states — Democratic and Republican — have also refused to comply with the government's demands. The Justice Department has sued all of them. The Trump administration says access to voter rolls will help purge the lists of immigrant voters who are not entitled to vote. The administration has alleged, without providing evidence, that 278,000 noncitizens are registered to vote. And a White House spokesperson has said that noncitizens "continue to register and vote in federal elections." Noncitizen voting does happen, but it's extremely rare. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said this summer that thousands of noncitizens were mistakenly registered in her state due to a software glitch. About 340 of them actually voted. Since the beginning of Mr. Trump's second term, the Justice Department has charged more than 100 noncitizens with voting illegally. Henderson said she found just 52 questionable voters on the rolls out of more than 2 million registered voters in Utah. DHS Secretary Mullin this summer said that any election official who knowingly allows noncitizens to vote could be prosecuted, or even sent to prison." "We're not going to prison. No. It's silly," Henderson said. Last month, in writing, the Justice Department told Henderson she was under investigation. "I have to tell myself it doesn't matter what the consequences are, as long as I feel like I'm doing what's right," she said. "I think this is an important thing for me to do, holding these guard rails, holding the line. Someone has to." Henderson believes there can still be honest and fair elections. The question for her is whether the losing candidate will accept the results. "We are seeing a trend of candidates who lose races now refusing to concede, saying it was rigged, saying it wasn't fair, even when it isn't close," she said. "Candidates who lose can do so much good by graciously conceding. That will instill confidence in the public." "I never imagined that we would be raided by the FBI" In January, armed federal agents seized ballots from a local facility in Fulton County, Georgia. "In my wildest dreams, I never imagined that we would be raided by the FBI," Fulton County Commissioner Dana Barrett, a Democrat, told 60 Minutes. The agents had a criminal search warrant that Georgia's secretary of state described as being full of "baseless and repackaged claims," but it enabled them to seize ballots and other election materials from the 2020 election, which Mr. Trump has repeatedly claimed he won. Federal agents in Fulton County packed up more than 600 boxes of election records. Then director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, watched as boxes of ballots were loaded onto trucks. Barrett has no idea where the ballots are now. She believes the seizure was "political theater aimed at undermining the 2026 and 2028 elections." "I think it was all part of this concerted effort that's happening nationwide to undermine faith in elections," Barrett said. Three months ago, the FBI temporarily reassigned 260 analysts to work on a "priority investigation" into the Georgia materials, according to an internal FBI email obtained by 60 Minutes. So far, nothing has come of the investigation. There have been dozens of probes into the 2020 election in Fulton County, but none have moved the needle. "People see all of these investigations and FBI raids and subpoenas and they say, 'Something must be wrong there. Why should I believe the results?'" The Justice Department responds Dhillon, the head of the Civil Rights Division of the Justice Department, said the administration is aggressively pursuing new investigations and they are looking at "thousands" of possible cases of noncitizen voting. "We've been in office for less than two years. We've had investigations ongoing for over a year and it takes time," Dhillon said. Dhillon said there have been irregularities during prior elections, and that a record number of election observers and monitors – more than 1,000 of them – would be at the polls during midterms as a way to increase voter confidence. Recent surveys show that only about half of Americans expect the midterms to be free and fair. Dhillon called concerns that Mr. Trump might challenge midterm results "paranoia." If a noncitizen votes, that individual vote would be challenged, she said, not the entire election. "I don't know what is going to happen," Dhillon told 60 Minutes, "but I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states." item.title: France's unrest reaches the Louvre after weekend of violence and mass arrests
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Protests such as this one in Lyon rocked France over the weekend (Jeff PACHOUD) Protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre in Paris on Monday, as French authorities scrambled to stem public discontent fuelling mass cost-of-living demonstrations that over the weekend spilled over into some of the worst street violence in recent years. President Emmanuel Macron ordered a security review as the country's interior minister admitted that the police "had lost control" during the weekend's unrest. Undeterred, the Yellow Vests movement which organised the weekend's rallies called for a new round of protests Saturday. Italy, Spain and Portugal, where anger over rising prices has also led to protests, were keeping a nervous eye on the developments after smaller clashes broke out in Milan over the weekend and protests about housing costs persisted in Spanish cities. Some half a million people turned out across France to protest the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with high school students demanding better conditions at their schools. What started as peaceful demonstrations morphed into violence in some places, as masked groups on the sidelines of the protests attacked law enforcement, broke into town halls and other public buildings, setting many of them ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters on the streets. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered to resign on Monday after more than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured. Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator's hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade. "On Saturday, in some major cities, you couldn't look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn't lost control," Nunez said. Macron refused Nunez's resignation, even as he acknowledged security and intelligence failures in the government response, despite the some 60,000 law enforcement personnel deployed across the country on Saturday. Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70 percent of whom were adults, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said Monday. More than 2,000 shops were expected to have been affected by the weekend's violence across France, with damage running into "hundreds of millions of euros", according to chamber of commerce president Alain Di Crescenzo. In an address to the nation Sunday evening, Macron slammed the "unbridled" violence and said local authorities would be able to ban -- "if necessary" -- certain rallies in coming days. But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew. City authorities in Marseille said on Monday that public gatherings would be banned from noon to 08:00 pm (1000-1800 GMT). - Louvre blocked - The public discontent showed no signs of subsiding on Monday, with demonstrators blocking the entrance to Paris's iconic Louvre Museum, the most visited in the world. "We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world's largest museum," read a leaflet posted outside the museum, as management and unions said the protest was led by students from Ecole du Louvre. Rising prices have fuelled anger in France, where diesel prices have jumped nearly 40 percent and petrol by 25 percent since March and where food prices have risen by 25 percent since 2021. - Elections - The unrest in France has flared just months before a key presidential election where centrist Macron cannot stand again and Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, is riding high in the polls. Ministers have blamed "ultra-left" groups for the violence, while Le Pen claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Melenchon, had "legitimised the violence". The left has accused Macron of ignoring protesters' demands, while the right is calling on him to take a firmer line. - Europe - With costs of living rising across Europe, smaller demonstrations have broken out in other countries. During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan, with Mayor Giuseppe Sala warning: "I'm very worried because it's a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself." In Spain, hundreds of tents have occupied Madrid's central Puerta del Sol square since September, when the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong flat sparked nationwide protests in a country with soaring housing costs. Dozens of tents have also sprung up in Portugal's main cities of Lisbon and Porto, with protesters demanding action over rising costs of housing. burs/yad/ekf/gv This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/police-lost-control-during-french-074439816.html

item.title: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane hits another dead end after 89 years
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A mysterious object discovered near a remote Pacific island is not the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's missing plane , researchers said after an expedition to the site, dealing another setback to efforts to solve one of aviation's greatest mysteries nearly 90 years after the pilot disappeared. "Evidence gathered at the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro confirmed that the visual anomaly first seen in satellite imagery in 2020 was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit," the researchers said . "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment," which they said is what they had initially hoped was the plane. The researchers said the reflective surface of the anomaly, which had led them to believe it could be metal, was the result of a carbonate veneer, noting other items found nearby were "similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand." On Oct. 14, a 17-member expedition team led by Purdue University's Steve Schultz and the Archaeological Legacy Institute's Richard Pettigrew launched an expedition to investigate a mysterious object that in aerial photos appeared to resemble possible wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane. Severe weather kept the research team aboard their ship for three of the five days allotted for the search, while limited fuel and supplies prevented them from extending the expedition. The search area was so remote, it took the team five days at sea to reach it. The expedition focused on a lagoon off Nikumaroro, where researchers examined the Taraia Object, an anomaly spotted by a Navy veteran in satellite imagery during the COVID pandemic. Although visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938, the object went unnoticed until 2020. Pettigrew said before reaching it that they believed it could be metal rather than a tree, but further investigation was needed to confirm its identity. "Amelia Earhart's spirit of courage and curiosity drove every step of the search," Pettigrew said Sunday. "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we're deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible. Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished." The team had developed plans to photograph and film the lagoon and Taraia Object before using magnetometers and sonar equipment to survey the area. Researchers then planned to retrieve the object for identification. The Archaeology Channel documented the expedition through short video updates on its Heritage Broadcasting Service streaming platform. The research team previously said in a news release that there was "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane. Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared on July 2, 1937, roughly 22,000 miles into their trip. Earhart was attempting to become the first female pilot to circle the world, and the first pilot to do so around the equator, Earth's widest point. Recently, President Trump ordered the declassification of records related to Earhart . Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island lies about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were headed when they disappeared during their attempted flight around the world. Pettigrew believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro and survived there for some time. He points to relics dating to the 1930s and to human remains discovered on the island, which were later lost as possible evidence. However, several competing theories about the aviator's disappearance have emerged over the decades, many of which lack conclusive evidence. Researchers have spent decades searching for Earhart's plane, hoping its discovery could shed light on her disappearance. In 2024, an expedition team captured a sonar image of what appeared to be an aircraft on the ocean floor, but the object was later identified as a rock formation. Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fire Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured at a base in the province of Alberta after a fire broke out in a grassy training area and spread rapidly due to strong winds. Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. "The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died. Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening. Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC. Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing. "There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition. A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range. "What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area." Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there. News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation. Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable". The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said. In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference". [BBC] Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright. The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down. What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units. "It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province. STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed. Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, were killed in the incident, which unfolded shortly before 3:30 p.m. at the city-owned Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, police said. The deceased were both from McPherson, Kansas, but were not related to each other, a Wichita police spokesperson said. Ten other people, ages 5 to 68, were also hit and hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries, Police Capt. Aaron Moses said. Police said a dark Chevrolet pickup drove onto a field during a youth soccer game and struck children and adults. Erica Case said it was halftime during her 9-year-old son’s soccer game on an adjacent field when she first heard an engine revving, followed by several “boom” sounds. “I saw the truck hitting things. I saw debris flying in the air,” she recalled. “I don’t know if it was a cone, a chair or a person, but you could see matter flying as the truck was barreling through the soccer field at a decent rate of speed.” She said the sound will haunt her. “The moment that I recognized that that wasn’t gunshots, that that was bodies, I lost it,” Case said. “I lost it because it wasn’t just adults. It was also children.” Police were investigating what caused the pickup truck to barrel through a soccer field, killing a man and a child. (David Griekspoor) Case recalled the mother of another boy shouting that she was a nurse and needed to get to the injured. Case said she told her she would watch her boy and then took the woman’s son to safety amid the chaos. It took about 10 minutes for emergency services to arrive, she said, but people began helping the victims during that time. “There are a lot of silent heroes that I know experienced much worse than I did, having to do mouth-to-mouth or CPR on somebody that’d been ran over by a truck,” Case said. David Griekspoor was at the complex with his nephew, who also plays soccer, when he witnessed the incident. “It sounded like small gunfire,” he said. “Bap, bap, bap.” He said it wasn’t clear what was producing the sound until he focused on the truck. “You look up, and you just see the truck going through a line of people,” Griekspoor said. He said his brother and sister-in-law went to check on children nearby as he grabbed his nephew and “backed out of there.” All ended up safe, Griekspoor said. Police said they interviewed more than 30 witnesses. The pickup’s driver, a 34-year-old woman from Garden City, Kansas, was taken into custody but was later released after police consulted with the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office. She has not been charged with a crime and has not been identified. Police said the woman, who had two children in the pickup, had a child who had a soccer game on a different field at the complex. The driver was cooperating with officers, said Moses, the police captain. What caused the pickup to drive through the field was still under investigation, and police said the results of an examination of the vehicle, as well as of toxicology testing on the driver, were pending. item.title: Vance says 'there's a chance' he won't run for president in 2028
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Vice President JD Vance (Daniel Heuer-Pool/Getty Images) Despite leading early polls of potential 2028 Republican presidential candidates, Vice President JD Vance says "there's a chance" he won't enter the race. Speaking during a CBS News town hall Saturday in Flat Rock, Michigan, Vance acknowledged that family considerations could influence whether he seeks to succeed President Donald Trump. "Of course there's a chance," Vance said when asked whether he might sit out the 2028 presidential election. "We've got four little kids, my wife has never loved politics. She loves public service.” The vice president's comments came despite his substantial lead in early Republican presidential primary polls. According to the RealClearPolling average, Vance leads the potential 2028 Republican presidential field with 39% support, 15 percentage points ahead of Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son, ranks third with 11%. Trump previously described Vance as his "most likely" successor, although the vice president says he has not decided whether to seek the nomination. Vance told CBS News anchor Tony Dokoupil that he tends to put off major personal decisions. "The way that I think about life, big life decisions — my wife will tell you this: I'm a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it," Vance said. He indicated that he and second lady Usha Vance would discuss their political future more seriously after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. "Whenever it comes up, it's always let's figure it out after the midterms," Vance said. The couple welcomed their fourth child, Alec, in July. They also have three older children, Ewan, Vivek, and Mirabel. Usha Vance previously acknowledged that she and her husband don't always share the same political views. "Sometimes I have thoughts that fit very comfortably into one side or another," she told NBC News in March. "Sometimes I have views that are way more idiosyncratic." She emphasized that she serves as a sounding board for her husband rather than as a political adviser. During the town hall, Vance faced questions about rising gasoline prices, immigration enforcement, and the Iran war, defending the administration's policies while acknowledging that Americans continue to face economic challenges. Vance said his immediate priority is helping Republicans retain control of Congress, including campaigning for former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan's competitive Senate race. "We're really not" discussing 2028, Vance said of conversations with his wife. "Anything could happen, man." © 2026 Newsmax.
